doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Rhythm tracks, scratch vocals and playing live off the floor
summary: Artists were present for rhythm tracks with scratch vocals; he compares Motown crowding, headphones, live strings and direct-to-disc pressure.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: And you’d usually hear a demo, but when you were recording the background track —
The rhythm track, were you hearing a singer?

Yes. If it wasn’t the artist there would be somebody in there, they called it, “the scratch vocal.” Usually the artist was there. I can think of only a few occasions if something happened and we had to cut a track without the artist being there. The artist was always there. Anywhere. On either coast. And yeah, they’d be in the booth doing their scratch vocal, but a lot of times we would nail it on the first take. The rundown. And we’d do a second. We’d do the rundown, then take 1, take 2, and go back and keep the rundown.
And sometimes the vocals were that way too.
Everybody playing at the same time.

Yeah. And if you’ve seen “Standing in the Shadows of Motown” where everybody was crammed in that one room, and sometimes with strings and brass and background singers, I mean just crammed into one room, and they weren’t wearing headphones. By the time I started playing everybody was wearing headphones. We’d be in a room together and usually it was a five piece rhythm section, six piece rhythm section, but I also did things where we were live with strings and — sometimes strings, brass and woodwinds. And that was in LA for big dates. And you just — you can’t screw up. You don’t want to be the guy that makes them start over again. Especially, I came along when there were still guys playing when it was direct to disk. And if you screwed up it goes in the trash can. Put another disk on and cut — it was not going to tape in the old old days, it was going to disk. A lacquer. And literally they’d be throwing them in the trash can the guys told me. And I did some direct to disc recording in LA and I mean always the pressure was on but you didn’t show it and you just had to deliver really quick. And that’s another thing, it’s the quick mind, the quick inventive mind, creative mind. You’d have to create those licks, memorable licks, on the spot. Especially guitar players and keyboard players.
